stored: mixed; the two stored sources are a narrative review and a rat study, with no human intervention estimate
as_read: Conflicting with no clear benefit: the two largest cardiovascular syntheses and two PSA meta-analyses are null; older blood pressure pooling and small trials are positive.

quote.text: Overall, the findings showed that lycopene and tomato consumption did not affect cardiovascular risk factors.

proposed_decision_text: The labels print lycopene at 2 mg to 50 mg, and three name Lyc-O-Mato. A meta-analysis of 34 randomized trials found lycopene and tomato consumption did not affect blood pressure, lipids, glucose or inflammatory markers, apart from lower malondialdehyde (PMID 37496241). A review of 43 intervention studies at 1.44 to 75 mg a day found no significant difference for blood pressure or lipids and calls the findings conflicting (PMID 32652029). Two meta-analyses of six trials each found no overall effect on PSA (PMID 33355018, PMID 35031434). Evidence on the other side exists: earlier pooling found lower systolic pressure with lycopene (PMID 28129549, PMID 24051501), a tomato nutrient complex lowered systolic pressure at 15 mg and 30 mg of lycopene while 15 mg of synthetic lycopene and 5 mg of the complex did not (PMID 31035474), 7 mg a day improved endothelial function in cardiovascular patients but not in healthy volunteers (PMID 24911964), and 25 mg raised sperm count in 44 men with oligozoospermia (PMID 31468596). A small meta-analysis found modest sperm concentration gains (PMID 40806357). This is an abstracts-only review. The stored sources, a narrative review and a rat study, give no human estimate (PMID 27840359, PMID 36422550). Taken together the evidence conflicts with no clear benefit, so this review earns no credit.
